title: Robustness Verification for Checking Crash Consistency of Non-volatile Memory
problem: Programs using non-volatile memory (NVM) must explicitly flush pending stores to guarantee persistence; developers routinely miss or mis-order these flushes. Existing crash-consistency checkers are testing-based and require user guidance, leaving the correctness of NVM programs unverified in the general case.
motivation: As NVM technologies (e.g., Intel Optane) are deployed in production systems, undetected crash-consistency bugs can silently corrupt persistent data structures, making a fully-automated, sound verification method urgently needed.
method: The tool proves that checking whether a particular memory state could result from a crash is equivalent to checking whether the execution is valid under additional ordering constraints. It searches all possible partial pre-crash executions and post-crash memory states, using an SMT solver (an automated logic-solving tool) to verify each combination by symbolically encoding the program. The DPLL(T) framework speeds up the search by eliminating impossible branches, and the approach is implemented in the tool PMVerify.
key_novelty: The key idea—reducing crash-consistency verification to an SMT reachability problem under the NVM memory model—enables the first fully automated robustness verification without user-written test inputs.
contributions: Formal definition of robustness as a crash-consistency property for NVM programs.
Algorithmic reduction of post-crash state reachability to memory-model-constrained execution validity, enabling SMT encoding.
PMVerify prototype integrating the algorithm into DPLL(T) for efficient exploration.
Experimental validation on PMDK benchmarks showing competitive bug detection vs. PSan (state-of-the-art dynamic tool).

metrics.other: Bug detection competitive with PSan on PMDK benchmarks

limitations: Scalability to large NVM programs with complex data structures is not discussed.
